item.content:encoded:
NASA has released the final Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute Cooperative Agreement Notice-5 (SSERVI CAN-5), inviting multi-institutional research teams to compete for major cooperative agreement awards supporting lunar science, planetary exploration, NASA’s Artemis programme and research that uses the Moon to prepare for future exploration of Mars.

The final opportunity is:

SSERVI CAN-5 – NNH26ZDA016C

NASA’s Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate are jointly supporting the initiative. The call seeks integrated, multi-institutional teams capable of advancing fundamental and applied research on the Moon and its near-space environment, while strengthening connections between planetary science and human exploration. “Mars forward” projects that use lunar research to develop approaches relevant to eventual Mars exploration are explicitly welcomed.

The funding opportunity is particularly notable because teams can combine major scientific research with activities designed to strengthen the future STEM workforce and broaden public participation in NASA science.

The detailed CAN funding structure anticipates:

  • Approximately five awards
  • Up to approximately $1.8 million per year per team
  • An anticipated five-year award period
  • Approximately $9 million total per selected team over five years
  • Up to an average of $180,000 per year within the overall team budget for Workforce Development and/or Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps activities

The $180,000 is important to understand correctly: it is not an additional $180,000 on top of the $1.8 million annual award. It is part of the overall annual team budget and can support the additional workforce and engagement components.

The proposal process has two stages:

Step-1 Proposal Deadline: September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM Eastern Daylight Time

Step-2 Full Proposal Deadline: December 4, 2026

Only teams that submit the required Step-1 proposal may proceed to Step 2. NASA will use dual-anonymous peer review, and applicants must submit their proposals through NASA’s NSPIRES system rather than through Grants.gov.

Important update about the earlier draft

The document initially circulated for community comment was DRAFT SSERVI CAN-5, NNH26ZDA013J. That draft was issued on July 10, 2026 and closed for comments on July 28. NASA has since issued the final call as NNH26ZDA016C, so applicants should use the final announcement number and final deadlines rather than the dates or placeholders contained in the draft.

This article therefore uses NASA’s final announcement for the current solicitation number and deadlines, while drawing on the detailed CAN documentation supplied with the opportunity for the programme’s research structure, funding architecture and proposal requirements.

About NASA’s Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute

The Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute, or SSERVI, is a distributed research institute that brings together expertise from the scientific and human exploration communities.

Its premise is that:

Science enables exploration, and exploration enables science.

SSERVI is designed to create collaborative research teams rather than fund a collection of isolated individual projects.

The Institute connects researchers working across areas such as:

  • Lunar science
  • Planetary science
  • Space physics
  • Human exploration
  • Geology and geophysics
  • Engineering
  • Biological and physical sciences
  • Robotics
  • Sample science
  • Space environments
  • Technology
  • Public engagement
  • Workforce development

Selected teams become participating members of the broader SSERVI network and are expected to collaborate both internally and across other Institute teams.

The Institute is coordinated through SSERVI Central at NASA Ames Research Center. Its virtual structure enables geographically distributed universities, research organisations, NASA institutions, industry partners and other eligible organisations to work together on large interdisciplinary problems.

What NASA Is Looking for Through SSERVI CAN-5

NASA is not seeking disconnected small projects under this call.

It wants:

Multi-institutional, team-based, integrated research programmes.

The final announcement specifies that proposals should present innovative basic and/or applied research that advances understanding of:

  • The Moon
  • The Moon’s near-space environment
  • Scientific questions relevant to human lunar exploration
  • Research required to enable Artemis
  • Lunar research that can inform future Mars exploration

NASA says proposals complementing current CAN-4 SSERVI teams, or filling important research gaps not already covered by the Institute, will receive strong consideration.

Supporting NASA’s Artemis Programme

A central objective of CAN-5 is supporting NASA’s return to the Moon through:

  • Human missions
  • Robotic missions
  • Lunar surface research
  • Sample science
  • Exploration science
  • Development of scientific approaches supporting longer-duration lunar activity

The Moon is therefore not treated solely as a scientific destination.

It is also regarded as a location where researchers can develop knowledge, methods and operational experience necessary for future human exploration.

The “Mars Forward” Approach

NASA explicitly welcomes:

Mars-forward research

This means proposals may use studies of the Moon to develop:

  • Methods
  • Scientific knowledge
  • Operational approaches
  • Exploration concepts
  • Technologies

that could later inform Mars missions.

The Moon can serve as an intermediate environment for studying issues such as:

  • Long-duration surface operations
  • Radiation
  • Dust
  • Resource utilisation
  • Habitat sustainability
  • Robotics
  • Autonomous operations
  • Human-machine interaction
  • Sample handling

NASA’s final announcement specifically confirms that proposals using lunar-focused research to develop approaches to Mars exploration are welcome.

Anticipated Funding: Up to $1.8 Million Per Year

The detailed CAN funding table anticipates:

$9 million in first-year funding for all new awards

with approximately:

Five awards

at an anticipated level of:

$1.8 million per year for five years

or approximately:

$9 million per selected team over five years.

If five awards were funded at the anticipated maximum annual level across the full five-year period, the overall multi-year programme value could be substantial.

However, applicants should not interpret future-year funding as automatically guaranteed.

The detailed CAN notes that awards are generally not fully funded upfront and future-year funding depends on:

  • Congressional appropriations
  • Availability of NASA funding
  • Continued programme funding
  • Acceptable performance and award conditions

Applicants should therefore construct realistic five-year budgets while recognising the federal appropriations condition attached to out-year funding.

Up to $180,000 Per Year for Workforce Development, Citizen Science and Public Engagement

One of the most interesting features of SSERVI CAN-5 is its explicit integration of scientific research with wider workforce and community engagement.

The detailed CAN allows teams to request up to an average of:

$180,000 per year

across the proposed five-year period for the combined activities associated with:

  • Workforce Development Plan
  • Citizen Science Plan
  • Science Activation Plan
  • Space Apps Plan

Again, this amount is part of the overall SSERVI team budget rather than an additional award outside the main funding ceiling.

This provision creates an unusual opportunity for institutions that want to combine advanced lunar and planetary research with:

  • Student development
  • Postdoctoral training
  • STEM workforce development
  • Public participation in science
  • Science communication
  • Community engagement
  • Citizen science
  • NASA Space Apps activities

Workforce Development Plan

NASA places significant emphasis on preparing the next generation of researchers, scientists and engineers.

The Workforce Development Plan should describe how the team will:

  • Build knowledge
  • Develop technical or professional skills
  • Promote collaboration
  • Support professional growth
  • Prepare students and early-career researchers
  • Address changing workforce needs

The detailed CAN identifies possible activities such as:

  • Specialized undergraduate courses
  • Graduate courses
  • Workshops
  • Postdoctoral training opportunities
  • Field training
  • Internships
  • New degree programmes
  • Collaborative training initiatives

NASA also encourages partnerships that expand access to relevant knowledge and skills.

What the Workforce Development Plan Must Explain

The plan should clearly identify:

  • Objectives
  • Proposed activities
  • Approach
  • Expected outcomes
  • Potential impact
  • How the programme contributes to training future planetary scientists and engineers
  • How progress will be evaluated

An evaluation approach is required so the team can assess progress against its stated workforce objectives and identify areas for improvement.

Citizen Science Opportunities

SSERVI teams must also connect their activities with NASA’s broader public-engagement ecosystem.

The detailed solicitation allows proposals to include a:

Citizen Science Plan

A team may either:

  • Establish a new citizen-science project
  • Collaborate with an existing NASA-supported citizen-science project
  • Combine both approaches

Citizen science involves members of the public actively contributing to scientific research.

NASA expects these projects to maintain rigorous scientific standards and involve meaningful interaction between professional scientists and volunteers.

What a New Citizen Science Project Should Address

Teams proposing a new citizen-science initiative should explain issues including:

  • The relevant scientific field
  • Scientific questions being investigated
  • Citizen-science methodology
  • How the public contribution helps answer the research question
  • Why citizen science is an appropriate method
  • Relevant existing communities or platforms
  • Beta testing where necessary
  • Team expertise
  • How participants will be informed about project outcomes

The programme therefore treats citizen science as a genuine research method rather than simply a promotional activity.

Science Activation Plan

Teams can alternatively or additionally develop a:

Science Activation Plan

NASA’s Science Activation, or SciAct, approach aims to connect people of different ages and backgrounds with NASA science.

Activities might include:

  • Learning experiences
  • Workshops
  • Webinars
  • Educational resources
  • Training
  • Engagement with NASA subject-matter experts
  • Public events
  • Science experiences

The objective is to connect SSERVI-generated knowledge with established NASA Science Activation audiences and dissemination networks.

Space Apps Plan

Teams may also develop a:

Space Apps Plan

NASA’s International Space Apps Challenge is a global hackathon encouraging participants to use NASA data and resources to address challenges related to Earth and space.

A SSERVI team proposing a Space Apps component should consider developing relevant challenges and engaging subject-matter experts capable of supporting participants.

The detailed CAN indicates that Space Apps plans should explain:

  • The challenge idea
  • The problem participants will address
  • Desired outcomes
  • Relevant experts and support

A Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps Plan Is Expected

The detailed CAN states that SSERVI proposals should contain an engagement plan involving:

  • Citizen Science,
  • Science Activation,
  • Space Apps,

or some combination of these approaches.

Teams should identify a relevant liaison, subject-matter experts, personnel and corresponding budget.

This means public engagement is not simply an optional paragraph added at the end of the science proposal.

It is integrated into how NASA expects SSERVI teams to contribute to the wider scientific ecosystem.

Major Scientific Research Areas

The CAN supports a broad range of lunar and exploration research.

The detailed research list is explicitly non-exhaustive, meaning teams do not have to cover every area.

Potential research areas include the following.

Fundamental Lunar Geology

Research may examine:

  • Origin of the Moon
  • Internal structure
  • Mass anomalies
  • Core structure and formation
  • Surface evolution
  • Volcanic history
  • Tectonic history
  • Thermal evolution
  • Planetary differentiation
  • Lunar magma ocean
  • Crater distributions
  • Impact history
  • Earth-Moon system evolution

Lunar Environment

Research may examine the environmental conditions surrounding and affecting the Moon.

Possible subjects include:

  • Solar wind
  • Space weathering
  • Lunar exosphere
  • Plasma processes
  • Magnetic fields
  • Radiation environment
  • Effects of deep-space radiation
  • Effects of lunar albedo radiation on biological systems

Lunar Volatiles

The distribution and behaviour of volatiles are important both scientifically and for future exploration.

Potential research includes:

  • Origin of lunar volatiles
  • Chemical composition
  • Distribution
  • Transport
  • Sequestration
  • Regolith interactions
  • Volatiles in lunar samples
  • Permanently shadowed regions
  • Temperatures and lighting conditions
  • Depth and distribution of resources

Lunar Regolith

Regolith research is particularly relevant to future human and robotic surface activity.

Possible subjects include:

  • Formation and evolution
  • Particle size distribution
  • Geotechnical properties
  • Geochemistry
  • High-fidelity simulants
  • Robot-regolith interactions
  • Plume-surface interactions
  • Material extraction
  • Gas extraction
  • Partial-gravity effects
  • Regolith interactions with crop plants

Lunar Dust

Dust can affect:

  • Human health
  • Robotic equipment
  • Mechanical systems
  • Surface operations
  • Scientific instruments

Relevant research could examine:

  • Dust composition
  • Dust mobility
  • Particle size
  • Charge
  • Adhesion
  • Cohesion
  • Plasma-driven transport
  • Mechanical effects on systems

Returned Samples and Meteorites

SSERVI research can also include investigations involving:

  • Petrology
  • Geochemistry
  • Mineralogy
  • Geophysical properties
  • Magnetic properties
  • Geotechnical properties

of returned lunar samples and meteorites.

Sample Management

Relevant research may address:

  • Sample preservation
  • Storage
  • Collection
  • Return protocols
  • New analytical methods

Sample science is particularly significant as NASA prepares for future Artemis surface activities and potential sample return.

Cosmic Rays and Solar Storms

Proposals may study galactic cosmic rays and solar events in relation to:

  • Crew risk
  • Hardware risk
  • Mitigation approaches

Understanding the radiation environment is essential for longer-duration human activity beyond Earth.

Robotics, Automation and Autonomous Systems

Relevant areas may include:

  • Robotics
  • Sample handling
  • Automated analysis
  • Automated operations
  • Telerobotics
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Machine learning
  • Autonomous systems
  • Augmented reality
  • Virtual reality

The detailed CAN indicates that new technological approaches are welcome where they form part of a broader integrated scientific programme.

Planetary Protection

Possible areas include:

  • Survival of terrestrial organisms in extraterrestrial environments
  • Radiation exposure
  • Vacuum
  • Extreme temperatures
  • Microbial management
  • Antimicrobial approaches
  • Waste management
  • Prevention of microbial growth and spread

The Moon as a Scientific Platform

The unique lunar environment may also support research into broader astrophysical and fundamental-physics questions.

Examples listed in the CAN include:

  • Low-frequency radio astronomy
  • Dark Ages cosmology
  • Gravitational-wave concepts
  • Tests of general relativity
  • Cosmic-ray astrophysics
  • Observations uniquely enabled by the lunar environment

The programme therefore extends beyond conventional lunar geology.

Multi-Institutional Collaboration Is Required

A defining feature of the SSERVI model is collaboration.

Teams must involve expertise from:

More than one institution.

The programme also expects varied technical expertise rather than a team composed exclusively of researchers working in a single narrow subfield.

Research tasks should be intellectually connected.

A proposal that divides funding among unrelated projects without a convincing unifying research structure is unlikely to reflect the Institute model.

Who Can Apply?

This is primarily an institutional research funding opportunity, not an individual scholarship or personal fellowship.

Eligible entities identified in the detailed CAN include several categories.

Educational Organisations

Potentially eligible institutions include:

  • Public institutions of higher education
  • State-controlled universities
  • Private institutions of higher education
  • Independent school districts

Nonprofit Organisations

The detailed CAN lists:

  • 501(c)(3) nonprofit organisations
  • Eligible nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status

Government Organisations

Categories include:

  • State governments
  • County governments
  • City or township governments
  • Special district governments
  • Tribal governments

For-Profit Organisations

Eligible categories include:

  • For-profit organisations
  • Small businesses meeting relevant SBA size requirements

The detailed programme description also identifies research organisations such as universities, industry partners, FFRDCs, NASA Centers and other U.S. government agencies as part of the target research community.

Lead Institution Requirement

For multi-organisational proposals, one organisation serves as the:

Lead Institution

The detailed CAN states that this should be the:

Principal Investigator’s home institution.

NASA funding is provided to U.S. institutions under the solicitation framework.

The final public opportunity listing likewise states that proposers must be affiliated with institutions registered in NSPIRES and that NASA generally provides funding only to U.S. institutions.

Can International Researchers Participate?

Yes, but with an important distinction.

The opportunity is not structured as an internationally funded grant where institutions worldwide can independently lead and receive NASA funding.

Instead:

NASA generally provides funding to U.S. institutions.

International researchers and institutions may participate through collaborations conducted under NASA’s applicable no-exchange-of-funds rules.

The detailed CAN encourages U.S. proposers to collaborate with international researchers, including relevant existing SSERVI international partners and other appropriate organisations, while making clear that international lead institutions are not solicited.

Restriction Concerning China and Chinese-Owned Companies

The detailed CAN contains a specific institutional and national-participation restriction.

It states that proposals involving bilateral participation, collaboration or coordination with China or Chinese-owned companies, whether funded or under a no-exchange-of-funds arrangement, are ineligible for award under the solicitation.

Applicants involved in international partnerships should therefore read the final CAN and NASA Grants and Cooperative Agreements Manual carefully before building the proposal team.

Is Cost Sharing Required?

No.

The detailed CAN states:

Cost sharing is not required.

NASA may accept voluntary cost sharing, but it is not a prerequisite for competing for the award.

Two-Step Application Process

SSERVI CAN-5 uses a mandatory two-stage proposal process.

This is one of the most important requirements to understand.

Step 1: Preliminary Proposal

Step-1 proposals are due:

September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM EDT.

Submitting Step 1 is mandatory.

NASA’s final announcement confirms:

Only proposers that submit Step 1 are eligible to submit Step 2.

What Goes Into Step 1?

The detailed CAN describes Step 1 as a short preliminary summary.

The core submission uses the NSPIRES:

4,000-character Proposal Summary field.

No full budget is required at this stage.

NASA requests information including:

  • Principal Investigator
  • Institution
  • Contact details
  • Co-Investigators and known team members
  • Proposed project title
  • Brief investigation description

The Step-1 proposal must be submitted by the organisation’s Authorized Organizational Representative, or AOR.

Teams therefore need to involve their institution’s research administration office early.

Register Early in NSPIRES and SAM

Organisations and participating investigators need to be registered in:

NASA NSPIRES

NASA also notes that organisations must have valid System for Award Management (SAM) registration before registering in NSPIRES.

The detailed CAN warns that SAM registration can take significant time.

This makes early institutional coordination especially important.

Do not wait until September 29 to begin organizational registration.

Team Members Must Confirm Participation

The detailed application instructions also require relevant team members to confirm participation through NSPIRES.

A proposal cannot be submitted if required team members have not completed their participation confirmation and organizational relationship requirements.

This is another reason Principal Investigators should build their team early.

Step 2: Full Proposal

Full proposals are due:

December 4, 2026.

The final call uses:

Dual-Anonymous Peer Review

or:

DAPR

for proposal evaluation.

Step 2 is split into:

  • Volume A – Anonymous material
  • Volume B – Non-anonymous material

Anonymous Volume A

The detailed CAN identifies major components of Volume A including:

  • Proposal Cover Page
  • Table of Contents
  • Executive Summary
  • Research Plan
  • Anonymized Personnel and Work Effort Table
  • Redacted Budget and Narrative
  • Open Science and Data Management Plan
  • References
  • Workforce Development Plan
  • Fieldwork Plan, where applicable
  • Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps Plan

The draft specifies a substantial 35-page Research Plan, along with three-page limits for several specialized plans.

Applicants should consult the final CAN before submission for the definitive page and format limits.

Non-Anonymous Volume B

The detailed CAN describes the non-anonymous section as containing institutional and personnel information, including areas such as:

  • Team Collaboration and Science Management
  • Team agreements on acceptable behaviour
  • Fieldwork agreements where relevant
  • Contributions to SSERVI and NASA’s mission
  • Biographical sketches
  • Personnel and work-effort information
  • Current and pending support
  • Letters of commitment or support
  • Facilities and equipment information
  • High-End Computing information where required

NASA separates these materials from anonymous scientific content to protect the integrity of the dual-anonymous review.

Open Science and Data Management

SSERVI CAN-5 also places emphasis on:

  • Open science
  • Data management
  • Accessible research
  • Peer review
  • Responsible dissemination

Teams should therefore treat their data-management plan as a substantive component rather than an administrative afterthought.

Contribution to the Wider SSERVI Community

Selected teams are expected to contribute to the Institute beyond their own research programme.

Possible contributions may include:

  • Professional community development
  • Workshops
  • Seminar series
  • Cross-team collaboration
  • Research tools
  • Data visualisation
  • AI and machine-learning applications
  • Shared scientific facilities
  • Commercial space partnerships
  • International partnerships

The detailed CAN explicitly emphasizes that SSERVI is more than a collection of independent projects.

What NASA Will Evaluate

The final NASA announcement confirms that proposals will undergo peer review under the rules set out in the CAN.

Broad assessment considerations include:

  • Scientific and technical merit
  • Quality of the proposed research
  • Relevance to SSERVI
  • Relevance to NASA’s lunar and exploration priorities
  • Integration across disciplines
  • Open Science and Data Management
  • Workforce Development
  • Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps
  • Team collaboration and management
  • Cost reasonableness

The final call also gives strong consideration to proposals that either complement existing CAN-4 teams or address important gaps in the existing SSERVI research portfolio.

Application Timeline

The major confirmed dates for the final CAN-5 opportunity are:

Stage Date
Final CAN-5 available 2026
Step-1 proposal September 29, 2026, 11:59:59 PM EDT
Step-2 full proposal December 4, 2026
Anticipated award notification Approximately nine months after Step 2, according to the detailed CAN structure

NASA’s official final announcement confirms the September 29 and December 4 proposal deadlines.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through:

NASA NSPIRES

They cannot be submitted as applications directly through the Grants.gov synopsis.

Open the final SSERVI CAN-5 opportunity in NSPIRES

NASA’s current announcement number is:

NNH26ZDA016C

Applicants should use this number when searching NSPIRES.

For the NASA announcement explaining the final release:

Read NASA’s SSERVI CAN-5 final text announcement

Programme questions can be directed to:

HQ-SSERVI@mail.nasa.gov

NASA requests clarification questions sufficiently before the Step-2 deadline; the final announcement specifies that questions should be submitted no later than 14 calendar days before Step 2.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive SSERVI CAN-5 Proposal

1. Do Not Treat This as an Individual Research Grant

SSERVI wants a:

Multi-institutional team

with a coherent intellectual programme.

A collection of unrelated researchers and projects is unlikely to demonstrate the integration NASA is seeking.

2. Make the Artemis Connection Explicit

Explain exactly how the proposed science contributes to:

  • Understanding the Moon
  • Lunar exploration
  • Artemis
  • Future human exploration

Do not assume reviewers will make the connection themselves.

3. Explain the “Mars Forward” Value Where Relevant

If your research can help future Mars exploration, explain:

  • What lunar problem is being studied
  • What can be learned on the Moon
  • How that knowledge translates to Mars

A credible Moon-to-Mars logic can strengthen the proposal.

4. Build the Workforce Plan as a Real Programme

The workforce component can represent up to an average of $180,000 per year together with public-engagement activities.

Treat it as a serious programme with:

  • Objectives
  • Beneficiaries
  • Activities
  • Expected outcomes
  • Evaluation

rather than a generic promise to “train students.”

5. Think Beyond Traditional Outreach

CAN-5 creates opportunities to integrate serious research with:

  • Citizen science
  • Science Activation
  • Space Apps
  • Workforce development

Teams with strong science and thoughtful engagement structures can potentially create much broader impact than through conventional outreach alone.

6. Identify the Right Institutional Lead

Because funding is primarily directed through U.S. institutions, international research groups should identify an appropriate eligible U.S. lead partner early.

The lead structure needs to be determined before Step 1.

7. Register in SAM and NSPIRES Immediately

Administrative registration can derail an otherwise strong proposal.

Confirm that:

  • Lead organisation has SAM registration
  • Institution is registered in NSPIRES
  • PI is registered
  • Co-Investigators are registered
  • Team members establish required organizational relationships
  • Required participants confirm participation

well before September 29.

8. Protect Proposal Anonymity

NASA is using dual-anonymous peer review.

Applicants should therefore carefully remove identifying information from anonymous materials.

This includes more than simply deleting the PI’s name.

The detailed CAN cautions against revealing identity through:

  • Institution names
  • Logos
  • Self-identifying references
  • Named collaborations
  • Possessive descriptions of previous work
  • Pronouns revealing team-member identity

9. Review Existing SSERVI Teams

NASA says proposals complementing CAN-4 teams or filling gaps in existing research coverage will receive strong consideration.

Before designing the proposal, review what SSERVI already funds.

Ask:

  • What important scientific problem is missing?
  • How does the proposed work complement existing teams?
  • What new capability would this team add?
  • Why does the Institute need this team now?

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute Cooperative Agreement Notice-5

Abbreviation: SSERVI CAN-5

Final announcement number: NNH26ZDA016C

Agency: NASA

NASA directorates: Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate

Primary focus: Moon, lunar environment, Artemis and Mars-forward exploration research

Proposal model: Multi-institutional teams

Anticipated awards: Approximately 5

Indicative award level: Approximately $1.8 million annually per team

Indicative duration: 5 years

Indicative total per team: Approximately $9 million

Workforce/public engagement component: Up to an average of $180,000 per year within the total award budget

Cost sharing: Not required

Step-1 deadline: September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM EDT

Step-2 deadline: December 4, 2026

Review: Dual-anonymous peer review

Submission system: NASA NSPIRES

Programme contact: HQ-SSERVI@mail.nasa.gov

Conclusion

The NASA SSERVI CAN-5 2026 funding opportunity represents a major opportunity for universities, research institutions, nonprofits, industry partners, government research organisations and other eligible U.S.-based institutions to build ambitious multi-institutional teams focused on the future of lunar and planetary exploration.

Under final solicitation NNH26ZDA016C, NASA is seeking research programmes that can advance fundamental and applied understanding of the Moon and its near-space environment while contributing directly to Artemis and future human exploration. Mars-forward research using lunar science to develop approaches relevant to Mars is also explicitly encouraged.

The detailed CAN funding structure anticipates approximately five awards at around $1.8 million per year for five years, equivalent to approximately $9 million per team over the proposed award period, subject to federal appropriations and continued funding.

A particularly distinctive element is the opportunity to dedicate up to an average of $180,000 per year within the overall budget to Workforce Development and Citizen Science, Science Activation and/or Space Apps activities.

This creates room for institutions to combine frontier research with serious investment in:

  • Students
  • Early-career researchers
  • Postdoctoral scholars
  • STEM workforce pathways
  • Public participation
  • Citizen science
  • Science communication
  • Community engagement

Applications use a mandatory two-stage process. Step-1 proposals are due September 29, 2026, and only Step-1 proposers can proceed to the December 4, 2026 Step-2 deadline.

For teams working in lunar science, planetary science, human exploration, workforce development or meaningful public participation in NASA science, SSERVI CAN-5 is one of the most significant NASA team-research opportunities currently open.

The Agence Française de Développement (AFD) has opened the 2026 Call for Expressions of Project Intentions for Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), providing an opportunity for eligible civil society organizations to submit projects for potential AFD co-financing in 2027.

The call is designed to strengthen the contribution of civil society organizations to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), international solidarity, local development and policy change. For the 2026 edition, AFD has introduced a single call covering both French CSOs and locally governed CSOs, with the objective of identifying projects led by civil society organizations in partner countries that could receive financing in 2027.

The call is particularly relevant for eligible CSOs working on development, social transformation, international solidarity, climate vulnerability, civic engagement and other areas aligned with sustainable development priorities.

Applications must be submitted through AFD’s OSCar online platform, and organizations that do not already have an OSCar account must request account creation by September 15, 2026.

The final deadline for submitting project intentions is October 9, 2026, at 6:00 PM Paris time.

Overview of the 2026 AFD CSO Call

The 2026 CSO Call for Expressions of Project Intentions is part of AFD’s CSO Initiatives mechanism, which supports projects led by civil society organizations.

The mechanism recognizes the role of civil society in identifying development challenges and designing initiatives that respond to the needs of communities. Rather than limiting CSOs to projects defined by external institutions, AFD’s framework recognizes the right of initiative, allowing eligible organizations to propose projects that they have developed themselves.

For the 2026 call, AFD is seeking project intentions that can potentially be shortlisted for financing in 2027.

The initiative aims to achieve two closely connected objectives:

  1. Strengthen civil society organizations in France and AFD intervention countries.
  2. Generate concrete development impacts for beneficiary populations while contributing to local policy and sustainable development.

What Is the AFD CSO Initiatives Mechanism?

The CSO Initiatives (CSO-I) mechanism is an AFD financing mechanism for projects led by French and locally governed civil society organizations.

It is designed to support the capacity and effectiveness of civil society actors while enabling them to implement initiatives that contribute to development and international solidarity.

Through this mechanism, AFD can support CSOs that are working to address development challenges and create meaningful, measurable benefits for communities.

The mechanism is therefore particularly relevant to organizations that already have the institutional capacity, project experience and development-oriented mission needed to implement a substantial initiative.

Objectives of the 2026 Call

The 2026 call operates within France’s broader development and international solidarity framework.

It falls under France’s 2021 Framework and Programming Act on Development and International Solidarity, adopted on August 4, 2021. It also aligns with France’s Strategy for Civil Society and Civic Engagement for 2023–2027, the conclusions of the Presidential Council for International Partnerships from April 2025, and AFD Group’s 2025–2030 Strategy.

The call consequently forms part of a wider effort to strengthen civil society participation in sustainable development and international cooperation.

Key objectives include:

  • Supporting the role of civil society organizations in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.
  • Strengthening the institutional and operational capacity of CSOs.
  • Supporting initiatives developed by civil society organizations themselves.
  • Generating concrete benefits for communities and beneficiary populations.
  • Contributing to local policy development.
  • Supporting international solidarity and sustainable development.
  • Increasing the participation of locally governed CSOs in development financing.

Who Can Apply for the AFD CSO Call?

The call is open to eligible civil society organizations, rather than individual applicants.

Two broad categories of CSOs are relevant:

1. French Civil Society Organizations

French CSOs are eligible under the CSO Initiatives mechanism and can submit project intentions in accordance with the requirements of the call.

2. Locally Governed Civil Society Organizations

Locally governed CSOs in countries eligible for Official Development Assistance (ODA) can also be eligible for direct AFD financing under specific conditions.

This represents an important feature of the 2026 call because locally governed organizations are not automatically excluded from AFD financing simply because they are based outside France.

Eligibility Requirements for Locally Governed CSOs

According to the call, locally governed CSOs, including unions, are eligible provided that they have previously received financing at least once for a completed project from an eligible AFD Group entity or through certain qualifying mechanisms.

Previous financing may have been received:

  • Directly from the CSO-I mechanism.
  • Through AFD’s Operations Directorate.
  • From Expertise France.
  • From Proparco.
  • From the French Facility for Global Environment (FFEM).
  • From the Fund for Innovation in Development (FID).
  • Through an FSOF intermediary funding mechanism.
  • From a French embassy, where the annual financing received was more than €100,000.

The previous financing may have been received either directly by the locally governed CSO or through a lead CSO, provided the project has been completed.

The eligibility requirement applies regardless of the amount of qualifying AFD Group financing received.

This means that organizations should carefully review their previous institutional funding history before beginning the application process.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

The geographical scope of the 2026 AFD CSO call is broad.

Countries eligible for the opportunity are countries included on the OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) list of ODA recipients.

This means that eligibility is not restricted to one particular African subregion or a small group of countries.

However, the call gives priority to Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change.

Organizations operating in eligible developing countries should therefore examine how their proposed project responds to development needs, climate vulnerability and other strategic priorities.

Projects in France

Projects located in France may also be eligible, but under specific programmes:

  • Global Citizenship and International Solidarity Education (ECSI).
  • Civil Society Capacity Building (SMA).

Organizations proposing projects in France should therefore determine whether their project fits within one of these eligible programmes.

What Types of Projects May Be Relevant?

The call is intended for projects that contribute to sustainable development, international solidarity, civil society strengthening and concrete benefits for communities.

While the supplied call information does not provide a simple list of every eligible thematic sector, applicants should ensure that their proposed initiative clearly connects with the objectives of the CSO Initiatives mechanism and the broader development priorities reflected in the call.

Projects are particularly relevant when they:

  • Address clearly identified development challenges.
  • Respond to the needs of beneficiary populations.
  • Demonstrate potential for concrete and measurable impact.
  • Strengthen civil society participation.
  • Contribute to local policy or institutional development.
  • Support sustainable development objectives.
  • Address challenges affecting vulnerable populations.
  • Respond to climate vulnerability where relevant.
  • Demonstrate a strong understanding of the local context.
  • Are designed and led by civil society organizations with appropriate institutional capacity.

Important Funding Consideration

The 2026 call is a project financing and co-financing opportunity for eligible CSOs.

However, the information supplied for this call does not state one universal maximum grant amount that every successful applicant can receive.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that the programme offers a fixed amount of funding to every organization.

Instead, organizations should consult the official call documentation and methodological guide to understand the specific financing arrangements, co-financing requirements and financial conditions applicable to their proposed project.

How the Application Process Works

The application process is conducted through OSCar, AFD’s online platform dedicated to the submission of documents relating to the CSO Initiatives mechanism.

Project intentions submitted outside the OSCar platform will not be considered.

This makes it important for applicants to begin the administrative process early rather than waiting until the final deadline.

Step 1: Confirm organizational eligibility

Before preparing the project intention, the organization should determine whether it qualifies under the call.

Locally governed CSOs should pay particular attention to the requirement concerning previous qualifying financing and completed projects.

Step 2: Review the official call documentation

Applicants should carefully read the official call document and methodological guidance.

These documents provide important information about the procedures and requirements for preparing and submitting project intentions.

Step 3: Prepare an OSCar account

CSOs need a user account to access and use OSCar.

An authorization to use the platform is required when creating the account.

Organizations that already have an OSCar account should ensure that their account remains accessible and that the relevant users have the necessary permissions.

Step 4: Request an account if you do not already have one

Organizations that do not yet have an OSCar account must submit a request to create their account no later than September 15, 2026.

This is an important administrative deadline because it occurs before the final project submission deadline.

Organizations should not interpret October 9 as the only date they need to worry about.

Step 5: Prepare the project intention and administrative documents

Applicants should prepare the required project intention documentation and supporting administrative documents in accordance with the official templates and guidelines.

For locally governed CSOs, AFD provides a specific Project Intention Sheet.

Step 6: Submit through OSCar

The completed project intention and required administrative documents must be submitted directly through OSCar.

Only submissions made through the designated platform will be considered.

Important Application Deadlines

There are two important dates to remember for this call.

September 15, 2026 — OSCar Account Request Deadline

CSOs that do not already have an OSCar account must submit their account creation request by:

September 15, 2026

Organizations should therefore start the registration process well before this date.

October 9, 2026 — Final Project Submission Deadline

The final deadline for submitting project intentions is:

October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time

Applications must be submitted through OSCar before the deadline.

Waiting until the final hours could create unnecessary risks, particularly if organizations encounter account, document or technical issues.

Documents and Resources Available to Applicants

AFD has provided several resources to help CSOs understand and complete the application process.

1. 2026 Call for Expressions of Project Intentions

The official call document explains the framework and requirements for the 2026 CSO financing initiative.

2. Project Intention Sheet for Locally Governed CSOs

Locally governed CSOs can access the relevant project intention template provided by AFD.

3. Methodological Guide

AFD provides a methodological guide explaining the procedures for co-financing projects submitted by French and locally governed CSOs.

This guide can help organizations understand the recommended approach to preparing their project intention.

4. Authorization for Use of OSCar

Organizations creating an OSCar account need the relevant authorization document.

5. OSCar User Guide

AFD also provides a user guide explaining how CSOs can use the OSCar platform and follow the recommended submission procedures.

Applicants should make use of these resources before submitting their applications.

Why the Opportunity Matters for Civil Society Organizations

The AFD CSO call is significant because civil society organizations often have close relationships with communities and can identify challenges that may not always be visible through traditional institutional structures.

By recognizing the right of initiative, the mechanism gives eligible organizations an opportunity to propose projects based on their own understanding of development needs.

The call can therefore be particularly valuable for CSOs that have:

  • A strong record of community engagement.
  • Experience implementing development projects.
  • Established relationships with local communities.
  • Institutional experience with donor-funded projects.
  • Evidence of previous project results.
  • Capacity to manage project finances and reporting.
  • A clear development or international solidarity mission.
  • A project concept aligned with sustainable development priorities.

How to Prepare a Strong Project Intention

A competitive project intention should do more than describe a good idea.

The organization should demonstrate why the project is necessary, who will benefit, what will be achieved and why the organization is capable of delivering the proposed results.

1. Clearly define the problem

Begin by identifying the development challenge the project intends to address.

Explain:

  • What the problem is.
  • Who is affected.
  • Where it occurs.
  • Why it matters.
  • What evidence demonstrates the need for intervention.

2. Identify the beneficiaries

Clearly describe the populations that will benefit from the proposed project.

Where possible, explain the characteristics of the target population and why they require support.

3. Demonstrate local relevance

A strong project should be grounded in the realities of the country or community where it will be implemented.

Applicants should demonstrate that the organization understands the local context and has meaningful relationships with the communities involved.

4. Explain the proposed solution

Describe how the project will respond to the identified problem.

The proposed activities should logically connect to the expected results.

5. Demonstrate organizational capacity

Applicants should show why their organization is capable of implementing the proposed initiative.

Relevant evidence can include:

  • Previous projects.
  • Organizational experience.
  • Staff expertise.
  • Partnerships.
  • Previous donor funding.
  • Community relationships.
  • Previous project results.

6. Connect the project to sustainable development

Applicants should demonstrate how the proposed project contributes to relevant Sustainable Development Goals and broader development priorities.

7. Consider climate vulnerability

Because the call gives priority to countries particularly vulnerable to climate change, organizations in such contexts should clearly explain relevant climate-related challenges where appropriate.

8. Focus on measurable impact

Avoid presenting only activities.

Explain the expected changes resulting from the project and how those changes will benefit communities.

Key Advantages of the 2026 AFD CSO Call

The opportunity offers several important advantages for eligible civil society organizations.

Access to Potential Project Financing

Selected projects may be considered for AFD financing in 2027, giving eligible organizations an opportunity to secure support for development initiatives.

Support for Civil Society

The CSO Initiatives mechanism is specifically designed to strengthen civil society stakeholders and their ability to contribute to development.

Opportunity for Locally Governed Organizations

Eligible locally governed CSOs can potentially access AFD financing under the conditions established by the call.

Alignment with Global Development Goals

The mechanism is explicitly connected to the Sustainable Development Goals and international solidarity.

Potential Policy Impact

The initiative is also intended to contribute to local policy, meaning that well-designed projects can potentially influence wider systems and development approaches beyond individual beneficiaries.

Important Things Applicants Should Know

There are several details that applicants should not overlook.

This is not an individual scholarship or fellowship

The opportunity is intended for civil society organizations, not individual students, researchers or job seekers.

Individuals cannot apply in their personal capacity unless they are applying on behalf of an eligible organization in accordance with the call requirements.

Previous financing matters for locally governed CSOs

Locally governed organizations should carefully examine the previous-financing requirement before investing substantial time in preparing a submission.

The OSCar account deadline comes first

Organizations without an existing OSCar account must request one by September 15, 2026.

The final deadline is October 9, 2026

The complete project intention must be submitted by October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time.

External submissions are not considered

Project intentions must be submitted through OSCar. Sending the project through another channel does not satisfy the application requirement.

Official Application Platform

Eligible organizations should submit their project intention through the official OSCar platform.

Access the OSCar application platform

Organizations that need to create an account should begin the process as early as possible and observe the September 15, 2026 account-request deadline.

For additional guidance, applicants can consult the official AFD call documentation and methodological resources.

View the official AFD 2026 CSO Call

Contact and Further Assistance

Organizations requiring assistance with the OSCar platform can use the official OSCar contact channel provided by AFD.

Contact the OSCar team

Applicants should also consult the official documentation before contacting the support team, as many procedural questions are addressed in the available guides.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 2026 AFD CSO Call for Expressions of Project Intentions?

It is an annual AFD call through which eligible civil society organizations can submit project intentions for consideration for potential financing under AFD’s CSO Initiatives mechanism.

Who can apply?

Eligible French CSOs and qualifying locally governed CSOs can apply, subject to the specific requirements of the call.

Can individual people apply?

No. This is an organizational project financing opportunity intended for eligible civil society organizations rather than individuals applying in their personal capacity.

Can organizations from developing countries apply?

Yes, eligible locally governed CSOs in countries included on the OECD DAC list of ODA recipients may apply under the conditions established by AFD.

Which countries are eligible?

All countries eligible for official development assistance according to the OECD DAC list are included, with priority given to Least Developed Countries and countries particularly vulnerable to climate change.

Can organizations in France apply?

Yes. Projects in France are eligible under the Global Citizenship and International Solidarity Education (ECSI) and Civil Society Capacity Building (SMA) programmes.

What is the deadline?

The final deadline for submitting project intentions is October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time.

Is there an earlier deadline?

Yes. CSOs that do not already have an OSCar account must request account creation by September 15, 2026.

Where should applications be submitted?

Applications must be submitted directly through AFD’s OSCar platform. Project intentions submitted through other channels will not be considered.

Is the opportunity fully funded?

The information provided does not describe the opportunity as a universal fully funded programme or specify one fixed funding amount for every successful applicant. Organizations should consult the official call documents for the applicable financing and co-financing conditions.

Visit HERE to learn more about the AFD CSO Call for Expressions of Project Intentions.

Final Application Tips

Before submitting a project intention, eligible CSOs should consider the following checklist:

  1. Confirm that the organization meets the eligibility requirements.
  2. If locally governed, verify the previous qualifying financing requirement.
  3. Confirm that the proposed country or project location falls within the eligible geographical scope.
  4. Review the official 2026 call document carefully.
  5. Read the methodological guide.
  6. Prepare the required project intention documentation.
  7. Ensure that the organization has an active OSCar account.
  8. If an account is needed, request it before September 15, 2026.
  9. Make sure all required administrative documents are complete.
  10. Submit the project intention through OSCar before October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time.
  11. Avoid waiting until the final day to submit.
  12. Keep copies of all submitted documents and relevant confirmation records.

Conclusion

The 2026 AFD Call for Expressions of Project Intentions for Civil Society Organizations represents an important financing opportunity for eligible CSOs seeking to implement development, international solidarity and sustainable development projects.

The call is particularly notable because it brings together French and locally governed CSOs within a single 2026 call and provides a pathway for qualifying civil society organizations in ODA-eligible countries to seek potential AFD financing for projects that can be implemented in 2027.

Organizations considering this opportunity should pay close attention to the eligibility conditions, particularly the previous-financing requirement applicable to locally governed CSOs. They should also begin the administrative process early because organizations without an OSCar account must request account creation by September 15, 2026.

The ultimate project submission deadline is October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time. Since submissions must be made through OSCar, eligible organizations should prepare their documentation, review the official guidance and complete their submission well before the deadline.

For CSOs with strong community relationships, relevant project experience and a clearly defined initiative that contributes to sustainable development and concrete benefits for communities, this call provides an opportunity to put forward a project for potential AFD support in 2027.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the ICCROM Fellowship Programme 2027, offering experienced cultural heritage professionals the opportunity to undertake an independent period of research and study with the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property (ICCROM).

The Fellowship Programme is designed for senior professionals in cultural heritage conservation who want dedicated time to pursue research, exchange knowledge with an international professional community, access ICCROM’s specialist collections, and develop work capable of contributing new perspectives to heritage conservation.

Applications for the 2027 cycle opened on:

15 August 2026

and close on:

15 September 2026

Successful Fellowships will normally be undertaken during 2027, unless another arrangement is agreed with ICCROM.

The programme is open to qualified professionals who are nationals of an ICCROM Member State or who work in an organization located in an ICCROM Member State. Applicants must normally have at least a Master’s degree or higher in a field related to cultural heritage and at least 10 years of professional experience in the heritage field.

Fellows may undertake research at ICCROM headquarters in Rome, Italy, although a Fellowship may be conducted partly online where there is an appropriate justification.

Typical Fellowships last:

3 to 6 months

although ICCROM may consider another timeframe where the applicant provides a convincing justification.

Applicants should note an important financial condition: ICCROM does not currently provide financial support or a living stipend for Fellows because of budgetary constraints. Fellows are responsible for their own travel, accommodation and personal insurance. ICCROM nevertheless provides important institutional and research support, including office facilities, access to its internationally significant conservation library and archives, internet access and engagement with heritage professionals.

About the ICCROM Fellowship Programme

The ICCROM Fellowship Programme is an established professional research opportunity intended to enrich the international field of cultural heritage conservation.

Its purpose is to:

  • Bring fresh perspectives into ICCROM
  • Facilitate the exchange of knowledge and ideas
  • Encourage new lines of research
  • Strengthen professional relationships
  • Support research relevant to heritage conservation
  • Connect senior professionals with ICCROM resources and expertise

The programme is especially appropriate for experienced professionals who already possess substantial knowledge of their field and can independently develop a focused research project.

This is not primarily a training course for beginners or an entry-level internship.

Fellows are expected to arrive with an independent research agenda and use the period at ICCROM to advance it.

What Is ICCROM?

ICCROM is an international intergovernmental organization dedicated to the conservation of cultural heritage.

Its work involves areas such as:

  • Cultural heritage conservation
  • Heritage risk management
  • Capacity building
  • Research
  • Policy
  • Education
  • Emergency response
  • Collections
  • Sites and monuments
  • Conservation science
  • Heritage management
  • Sustainable development

Its international network includes 139 Member States, following San Marino’s accession as the 139th Member State in November 2025. ICCROM’s membership spans countries across Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, the Americas and Oceania.

The Fellowship Programme allows experienced researchers and practitioners from this global network to spend time engaging with the organization and its resources.

Why Apply for an ICCROM Fellowship?

One of the principal advantages of the Fellowship is the opportunity to step away from everyday professional responsibilities and concentrate on independent research in an environment dedicated specifically to cultural heritage.

A Fellowship can provide time and space to:

  • Develop an existing research project
  • Investigate a new question
  • Examine archival sources
  • Conduct literature-based research
  • Compare international conservation approaches
  • Develop policy recommendations
  • Strengthen a publication
  • Explore emerging heritage challenges
  • Build international professional relationships

The Fellowship is particularly valuable because researchers are placed within an international heritage organization rather than a conventional university department.

This creates opportunities to connect academic research with:

  • Conservation practice
  • Policy
  • Institutional experience
  • International cooperation
  • Capacity building

Access to One of the World’s Major Conservation Libraries

ICCROM highlights its specialist library as one of the most important resources available to Fellows.

The collection includes material in more than 70 languages and is regarded as one of the world’s major specialized collections in cultural heritage conservation.

Depending on the proposed research, Fellows may use these resources to examine subjects including:

  • Conservation theory
  • Restoration
  • Heritage science
  • Archaeology
  • Museum collections
  • Built heritage
  • Disaster risk
  • Heritage policy
  • Sustainable conservation
  • Education
  • Traditional knowledge
  • Climate-related heritage threats

Access to such a specialist collection can be particularly valuable for researchers working on comparative or international projects.

Access to ICCROM Archives

Fellows also receive access to:

ICCROM’s archives

where relevant to their research.

Archival work can help researchers investigate:

  • The development of international conservation practice
  • Historical heritage policies
  • Institutional cooperation
  • Past ICCROM programmes
  • Training and conservation approaches
  • Evolution of professional standards

Applicants whose proposed project depends on specific ICCROM holdings should explain this connection clearly in the research proposal.

Research Exchange With ICCROM Professionals

The Fellowship is also intended to create opportunities for intellectual exchange.

During the Fellowship, participants may interact with:

  • ICCROM staff
  • Other heritage professionals
  • Researchers
  • Practitioners
  • International experts

This exchange can help Fellows:

  • Test arguments
  • Receive new perspectives
  • Discover comparative examples
  • Develop future partnerships
  • Identify additional research questions

However, applicants must distinguish professional exchange from formal academic supervision.

ICCROM Fellows Conduct Independent Research

A particularly important condition of the programme is that:

Fellows are expected to conduct independent research.

Applicants cannot request an ICCROM staff member to serve as their research supervisor.

This means candidates should already possess the intellectual and professional experience necessary to:

  • Formulate their own research question
  • Design the research
  • Manage the project independently
  • Analyze material
  • Produce the intended outputs

The Fellowship is therefore best suited to established heritage professionals rather than researchers requiring close doctoral-style supervision.

Who Can Apply?

ICCROM welcomes individuals specializing in disciplines related to:

Cultural heritage

Applicants may work as:

  • Researchers
  • Teachers
  • Practitioners

The Fellowship is particularly aimed at senior professionals.

Candidates must satisfy several important requirements.

Master’s Degree Requirement

Applicants must hold at least:

A Master’s degree or higher

in an area related to cultural heritage.

Relevant fields may potentially include areas such as:

  • Conservation
  • Heritage studies
  • Archaeology
  • Architecture
  • Art history
  • Museum studies
  • Conservation science
  • Cultural resource management
  • Historic preservation
  • Anthropology
  • Heritage policy
  • Related disciplines

The exact eligibility of a degree depends on its connection to cultural heritage and the applicant’s proposed research.

Professional Experience Requirement

Candidates must have been professionally active in the cultural heritage field for at least:

10 years

This requirement demonstrates clearly that the ICCROM Fellowship is designed for experienced professionals.

It is generally not intended for:

  • Recent Bachelor’s graduates
  • Early-stage Master’s students
  • Entry-level heritage workers
  • Professionals with only a few years of relevant experience

Applicants should make their professional experience particularly visible in their CV.

Geographic Eligibility

Applicants must be either:

  • Nationals of an ICCROM Member State, or
  • Professionals working in an organization located within an ICCROM Member State

ICCROM’s official membership currently extends across a broad global network of countries.

Examples include countries in:

  • Africa
  • Asia
  • Europe
  • North America
  • Latin America and the Caribbean
  • Middle East
  • Oceania

Applicants should confirm that their nationality or employer location falls within the official Member States list before applying.

Official Member States list:
https://www.iccrom.org/about/overview/member-states/full-list

Language Requirements

Research during the Fellowship may be conducted in:

Any language

However, Fellows are expected to have good knowledge of at least one of ICCROM’s two official languages:

  • English
  • French

This requirement enables Fellows to participate meaningfully in professional exchanges and the institutional life of ICCROM.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable communicating professionally in English or French.

Research Topics

ICCROM welcomes proposals concerning:

Any research topic related to cultural heritage conservation and ICCROM’s mission.

The call is intentionally broad.

Applicants are not required to limit themselves exclusively to the priority themes.

However, applications that align strongly with ICCROM’s current Strategic Directions may receive preference during selection.

Priority Research Areas for 2026–2027

For the 2026–2027 biennium, ICCROM identifies two particularly important thematic areas.

1. Better Heritage Conservation and Risk Management Approaches

ICCROM is interested in research exploring how heritage conservation and risk management can respond more effectively to:

  • Social change
  • Emerging hazards
  • Climate change
  • Urbanization
  • Digital transition
  • Complex crises
  • New technologies

This priority reflects the fact that cultural heritage is increasingly exposed to rapidly changing and overlapping risks.

Heritage and Climate Change

Changing climate patterns create significant risks for heritage.

Potential areas of research may include:

  • Extreme weather
  • Flooding
  • Drought
  • Wildfires
  • Sea-level rise
  • Heat
  • Changing humidity
  • Climate-related deterioration
  • Climate adaptation for heritage institutions
  • Risk assessment

Researchers might examine both physical threats to heritage and institutional strategies for addressing them.

Heritage and Urbanization

Rapid urban development can create both opportunities and threats for cultural heritage.

Relevant research could potentially address:

  • Historic urban landscapes
  • Development pressure
  • Urban regeneration
  • Infrastructure
  • Community participation
  • Heritage planning
  • Sustainable cities

Applicants should link such projects clearly to conservation practice and ICCROM’s mission.

Heritage and Digital Transition

Digital technologies are rapidly changing how heritage is:

  • Recorded
  • Preserved
  • Interpreted
  • Shared
  • Managed

Research could examine areas such as:

  • Digital documentation
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Digital archives
  • Remote sensing
  • 3D technologies
  • Data management
  • Digital access
  • Emerging conservation technologies

ICCROM particularly encourages work considering innovative technologies where they contribute to improved conservation and risk management.

Heritage in Complex Crises

Cultural heritage can be exposed to multiple threats during:

  • Armed conflict
  • Natural disasters
  • Political instability
  • Humanitarian crises
  • Displacement
  • Economic disruption

Research may explore how institutions and communities can prepare for, respond to and recover from these situations.

Priority Area 2: Integrating Heritage Into Broader Policy Agendas

ICCROM also welcomes research examining how heritage can be more effectively incorporated into wider:

National and international policy frameworks.

This priority recognizes that heritage conservation cannot always operate as a separate policy sector.

Instead, heritage increasingly intersects with major policy areas.

Heritage and Climate Action

Researchers may investigate how heritage can be integrated into:

  • National climate strategies
  • Climate adaptation
  • Climate mitigation
  • Disaster planning
  • International climate policy

This can include both protecting heritage from climate impacts and examining how heritage knowledge may contribute to climate resilience.

Heritage and Sustainable Development

Another major area is the relationship between heritage and:

Sustainable development

Possible research might examine:

  • Community development
  • Sustainable tourism
  • Cultural industries
  • Local knowledge
  • Urban sustainability
  • Economic development
  • Social resilience
  • Heritage and the Sustainable Development Goals

The goal is to better understand how heritage can contribute to development rather than being treated only as an object requiring protection.

Heritage and Education

ICCROM also identifies:

Education

as a policy area in which heritage can play an important role.

Potential subjects include:

  • Heritage education
  • Youth engagement
  • Professional training
  • Public awareness
  • Heritage in school curricula
  • Community learning

How Applications Are Evaluated

ICCROM publishes six major selection criteria.

Understanding these criteria can help applicants prepare much stronger proposals.

1. Overall Quality and Clarity

The proposed research should be:

  • Clearly written
  • Logically organized
  • Well defined
  • Intellectually coherent

Avoid overly broad topics.

A three-to-six-month Fellowship requires a focused research question.

2. Research Need

The project should address an:

Identified knowledge gap.

Applicants should therefore explain:

  • What is already known
  • What remains unclear
  • Why the gap matters
  • Why additional research is needed

A proposal that simply summarizes an established topic will likely be less competitive.

3. Quality of Anticipated Results

Applicants should demonstrate how their expected findings will represent:

  • A useful development
  • A practical contribution
  • Intellectual progress
  • A meaningful advance

for the field of heritage conservation.

Results might potentially take forms such as:

  • Academic paper
  • Policy recommendations
  • Methodological framework
  • Professional guidelines
  • Comparative analysis
  • Research report

Applicants should be specific about anticipated outputs.

4. Feasibility

ICCROM evaluates whether the proposed research can realistically be completed using:

  • Available resources
  • ICCROM collections
  • Fellowship timeframe
  • Applicant expertise

A highly ambitious project requiring several years of fieldwork would probably not be appropriate for a three-to-six-month Fellowship unless the ICCROM period forms a clearly defined component of a larger project.

5. Dissemination Plan

Applicants must explain how their research findings will be shared with the:

Broader heritage conservation community.

Possible dissemination routes may include:

  • Open-access publication
  • Academic journal
  • Conference presentation
  • Professional workshop
  • Institutional briefing
  • Online resources
  • Training materials
  • Policy communication

ICCROM particularly encourages:

Open-access dissemination.

6. Relevance to ICCROM’s Strategic Directions

Applications connected with ICCROM’s current Strategic Directions receive preference.

For 2026–2027, candidates should pay particular attention to the priority themes concerning:

  • Heritage risk management
  • Climate change
  • Urbanization
  • Digital transition
  • Complex crises
  • Innovative technologies
  • Heritage and climate policy
  • Sustainable development
  • Education
  • Health and wellbeing

A proposal does not necessarily need to fit these themes to qualify, but a strong connection can improve strategic relevance.

Preparing a Competitive ICCROM Fellowship Proposal

1. Identify a Specific Conservation Problem

Avoid proposing a topic such as:

“Climate Change and Cultural Heritage.”

Instead, narrow it to:

  • A particular heritage type
  • Specific geographic context
  • Defined risk
  • Policy problem
  • Methodological issue

A focused question is easier to complete within the Fellowship period.

2. Explain Why ICCROM Is Necessary

Do not write a proposal that could just as easily be completed at home.

Explain what ICCROM offers that is particularly valuable.

This might include:

  • Specialist library holdings
  • Archives
  • International conservation literature
  • Institutional history
  • Comparative expertise
  • Professional exchange

3. Demonstrate Professional Experience

The programme requires at least 10 years in the heritage field.

Use your application to show how that experience positions you to undertake genuinely independent research.

4. Connect Research With Practice

ICCROM is strongly practice-oriented.

Where appropriate, explain how your research can improve:

  • Conservation approaches
  • Risk management
  • Policy
  • Professional practice
  • Institutional capacity
  • Community engagement

5. Build a Realistic Research Schedule

A strong proposal should demonstrate what will happen during each phase of the Fellowship.

For example:

  • Initial literature and archive review
  • Comparative analysis
  • Consultation and professional exchange
  • Drafting
  • Validation
  • Final output preparation

6. Develop a Strong Dissemination Plan

Do not leave dissemination as an afterthought.

Explain:

  • Who needs your findings
  • How you will reach them
  • Which platforms you will use
  • Whether materials will be open access
  • How the work can continue beyond the Fellowship

7. Prepare Your Funding Plan

Because ICCROM does not provide a stipend, applicants should consider funding before applying.

Potential routes may include:

  • Employer support
  • University research funds
  • External grants
  • Professional development funds
  • National heritage institutions
  • Personal resources

The absence of ICCROM financial support should be factored into the feasibility of the Fellowship.

Conclusion

The ICCROM Fellowship Programme 2027 offers an important research opportunity for senior cultural heritage professionals who want to spend dedicated time developing independent research while engaging with one of the world’s leading international organizations for heritage conservation.

The programme welcomes researchers, teachers and practitioners working across cultural heritage disciplines. Applicants must normally hold at least a Master’s degree in a heritage-related field and have at least 10 years of professional experience.

Research may address any topic connected with cultural heritage conservation and ICCROM’s mission. However, the 2026–2027 cycle gives particular preference to projects addressing improved conservation and risk-management approaches, climate change, urbanization, digital transition, complex crises and innovative technologies, as well as research integrating heritage into climate action, sustainable development, education, health and wellbeing.

Fellowships normally last three to six months and may be undertaken at ICCROM headquarters in Rome, with partial online arrangements possible when justified.

Fellows receive office space, a workstation, internet access and full use of ICCROM’s specialist documentation, library and archives. ICCROM’s conservation library includes holdings in more than 70 languages.

Applicants should nevertheless understand that this is currently a self-funded Fellowship. ICCROM does not provide a stipend, travel allowance or accommodation funding because of present budget constraints. Fellows must arrange and finance their own travel, accommodation and mandatory medical and accident insurance.

The application requires an updated CV, employer approval where applicable and three reference letters from people with direct knowledge of the applicant’s work.

Applications opened on 15 August 2026 and must be submitted by 15 September 2026.
